findings.title: Accidentally committed git submodule ('sentry-repo') pointing at the repo's own base commit
findings.body: The PR adds a file `sentry-repo` containing `Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a` — a gitlink (embedded submodule) referencing the base commit of this very repository. This looks like a local checkout accidentally committed as a submodule. It adds a bogus gitlink to the tree, will break or slow down `git clone --recursive` / CI checkout steps (the submodule has no .gitmodules entry), and has nothing to do with the feature. It should be removed before merging.

findings.title: Substring match treats negated queries like `!event.type:error` as error-focused
findings.body: `_is_error_focused_query` returns True whenever the raw query string contains the substring "event.type:error". A query that explicitly *excludes* errors, e.g. `!event.type:error` (the standard way to query non-error/transaction events in discover), also contains that substring, so it will be classified as error-focused and `count()` will be rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)` over transaction rows, where sample_weight is absent/zero — returning wrong (likely zero) counts. Similarly, a query merely mentioning the field in another context (e.g. inside a quoted message search) triggers upsampling. The check should parse the query or at least exclude negated occurrences instead of doing a raw substring search.

findings.title: Upsampling decision uses outer `dataset`/raw request query instead of `scoped_dataset` and the actual query string
findings.body: Inside `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` closes over the outer `dataset` variable and the helper reads `request.GET['query']` directly, ignoring both the `scoped_dataset` parameter and the `query` argument passed to `_get_event_stats`. In the dashboard-widget split path, `_get_event_stats` is invoked with modified queries — e.g. `(<query>) AND !event.type:transaction` for the errors split (with scoped_dataset=discover) and `(<query>) AND event.type:transaction` for the transactions split — and with a scoped_dataset that can differ from the outer dataset (e.g. discover while the outer dataset is metrics_performance). As a result the upsampling transformation is applied or skipped based on the wrong dataset and the wrong query text: the transactions-only split query can get upsampled counts (wrong numbers) and the errors-only split query can fail to get upsampled counts (undercounted). The check should use `scoped_dataset` and the `query` parameter actually being executed.

findings.title: upsampled_count sums sample_weight with no NULL fallback, zeroing out events stored without a weight
findings.body: The new `upsampled_count` SnQL function compiles to `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` and the surrounding comments state it 'assumes sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects'. That assumption does not hold: allowlisting is per-project, but error events ingested *before* the project was allowlisted (or ingested without client sampling) have no sample_weight, and stats queries routinely cover historical time ranges. For rows where sample_weight is NULL, `sum` will either ignore them or return NULL (which `toInt64` turns into 0), so `count()` on an allowlisted project will silently undercount — showing 0 or fewer errors than actually occurred — for any time bucket containing older events. The aggregate should fall back to 1 for missing weights, e.g. `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))`.

findings.title: upsampled_count is registered as a public function, exposing it to arbitrary user queries
findings.body: Unlike the neighboring private SnQL functions (e.g. the one above it with `private=True`), `upsampled_count` is registered without `private=True`, making it usable by any user in arbitrary Discover queries and datasets. Against datasets/contexts where the `sample_weight` column does not exist (transactions, etc.) this produces Snuba query errors surfaced to users, and it exposes an internal implementation detail as part of the public query API. It should be marked private and explicitly allowed only where the upsampling transformation injects it.

findings.title: invalidate_upsampling_cache is dead code; allowlist changes are stale for up to 60s with no way to invalidate, and the docstring contradicts the cache
findings.body: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined and documented as the mechanism to call 'when the allowlist configuration changes', but nothing in the codebase calls it, so allowlist edits always take up to 60 seconds to take effect with no escape hatch. Additionally, the docstring on `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` claims it 'reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time ... to ensure we always have the latest configuration state', which is directly contradicted by the 60-second result cache in the only caller. Either wire the invalidation into the option-change path or fix the misleading documentation.

findings.title: _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling silently swallows invalid data and drops a 0 sample rate
findings.body: The new factory helper wraps everything in bare `except Exception: pass` blocks and only sets `normalized_data['sample_rate']` when `client_sample_rate` is truthy. A malformed or non-numeric `client_sample_rate` in a test event is silently ignored (the test then runs against unsampled data, producing confusing count assertions rather than a clear failure), and an explicit rate of 0 is dropped by the truthiness check. For test infrastructure, silently ignoring invalid fixture data makes failing tests much harder to diagnose; it should raise or at least validate explicitly.

findings.title: Top-level eligibility function and its 60s caching behavior are never tested
findings.body: The unit tests exercise the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`) but never call the public entry point `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`. That function contains the PR's riskiest new logic — the cache key construction, the cache-hit short-circuit, and the combination of cached eligibility with the per-request dataset check — so regressions there (e.g. caching False forever, key collisions across project sets, ignoring the dataset check on cache hits) would not be caught by these tests.
